essays.title: The Internet Was Built for Humans. AI Agents Are Breaking That Assumption.
essays.excerpt: AI agents can browse websites, fill forms, and perform tasks. But the real challenge isn’t getting an agent to click a button.
essays.body:
AI agents can browse websites, fill forms, and perform tasks. But the real challenge isn’t getting an agent to click a button. It’s making that interaction reliable, secure, and authorized.

Imagine asking an AI agent to book a train ticket.

It opens the website, searches for your destination, selects a date, and prepares to book.

Then it hits a CAPTCHA.

Or a login wall.

Or a page that changes its layout halfway through the task.

Or a security system that mistakes its activity for a bot attack.

Suddenly, your supposedly autonomous assistant needs you to take over.

This isn’t just a problem with one AI model. It’s a collision between two systems built around very different assumptions: an internet designed primarily for human interaction and AI agents designed to interact with it on our behalf.

And that collision is becoming increasingly important.

1. Websites aren’t obligated to welcome AI agents

The promise of AI agents is compelling.

Instead of manually comparing products, filling out forms, or navigating multiple websites, you describe the outcome you want and let an agent handle the steps.

But websites have their own incentives and responsibilities.

They need to protect user accounts, prevent fraud, control automated traffic, respect licensing agreements, and maintain their infrastructure.

Those requirements don’t disappear because the software making a request uses an LLM.

In October 2026, The Verge reported that major services were restricting AI agents for reasons ranging from licensing to security and website policies. Financial services have also raised concerns about agents accessing customer accounts.

Read the report from The Verge.

From a website owner’s perspective, an unfamiliar automated session might be a legitimate assistant — or an attempt to scrape data, abuse an account, or make unauthorized transactions.

The website often cannot safely assume the former.

The important distinction is that an agent’s ability to access a website does not automatically mean it has permission to perform every action on that website.

That is a product-design problem, a security problem, and an infrastructure problem.

2. Making an LLM smarter won’t solve every browser failure

A common approach to improving browser agents is to improve the model, provide better prompts, or give it more tools.

These techniques can help. But they don’t address every failure mode.

Consider four different problems:

Problem 1: The interface changes.

A button moves, a modal appears, or a website changes its layout. An agent relying on an outdated assumption may click the wrong element or fail to find it.

Problem 2: The website rejects the session.

A security challenge, rate limit, or authentication requirement can prevent the agent from proceeding. Better reasoning cannot grant permission that the website has withheld.

Problem 3: The page contains malicious instructions.

A webpage might contain text designed to manipulate an AI agent into ignoring its original task or disclosing information. Browser agents must treat website content as untrusted input, not as an authority that can override their instructions.

Google’s Chrome security team has discussed indirect prompt injection and the need for layered defenses in agentic browsing. Read Google’s security overview.

Problem 4: The agent makes a mistake but doesn’t recognize it.

It might submit an incorrect form, select the wrong item, or believe a task is complete when the final state says otherwise.

These are different problems. They need different solutions.

A single retry mechanism or a more powerful model won’t reliably fix all four.

3. The missing layer: reliable agent execution

A browser agent shouldn’t be judged solely by whether it can produce a sequence of clicks.

It should be judged by whether it reaches the intended outcome, respects permissions, and correctly identifies when it cannot proceed.

That requires an execution system around the model.

I would break this system into five components.

A. Observation

The agent needs an accurate view of the current page.

That might include a screenshot, accessibility information, DOM structure, visible text, or a combination of these signals.

It also needs to distinguish what it believes is happening from what it has actually observed.

B. Action

Every browser action should be explicit and traceable.

The system should know which element was targeted, what action was attempted, and whether the browser accepted it.

For consequential actions, the system should enforce appropriate approval requirements rather than trusting the model to decide everything.

C. Verification

After an action, the agent should check the resulting state.

If it clicks a button to submit a form, it should verify the submission rather than assuming success.

This is a fundamental difference between an agent that merely executes instructions and one that can demonstrate that the intended result occurred.

D. Recovery

When something fails, the agent needs to identify the failure category.

A missing element might justify re-observation. A temporary network error might justify a limited retry. An authorization failure should trigger a stop or an appropriate request for human intervention.

A CAPTCHA or explicit access restriction should not automatically trigger an attempt to circumvent the site’s controls.

E. Observability

Developers need to reconstruct what happened during a run.

That means recording relevant actions, observations, timestamps, errors, state transitions, and model decisions, with sensitive information redacted.

Without this information, debugging an agent can become an exercise in guessing.

Cloudflare’s Browser Run illustrates the growing infrastructure around agentic browsing, including browser sessions, recording, replay, and human intervention.

The broader lesson is that a reliable agent needs more than a model and a browser. It needs a system that can observe, verify, recover, and explain.

4. We need better ways for websites and agents to communicate

Today, developers often have to choose between different interaction methods.

They might use a documented API, interact with a website through browser automation, or use an agent-specific interface when one is available.

Each has trade-offs.

APIs can provide structured and predictable interactions, but they might not expose every workflow a user can perform.

Browser automation can interact with existing interfaces, but it is vulnerable to layout changes, session restrictions, and ambiguous page states.

Agent-specific interfaces could expose structured actions with clearer permissions and more predictable outputs. But they also require websites and agent platforms to agree on how those actions should be represented and secured.

This is why emerging browser-agent interfaces are worth watching.

For example, WebMCP documentation from Chrome discusses security considerations for structured tools exposed to agents through the browser.

I don’t think the answer is to make every website accessible to every agent.

Website owners should retain control over access, data, and consequential actions.

Instead, we need clearer ways to express:

  • Which agents are making requests.
  • What a particular agent is authorized to do.
  • Which actions require explicit user approval.
  • How websites can safely expose supported workflows.
  • How agents should respond when permission is denied.

The goal should be predictable, authorized interaction — not unrestricted automation.

5. How should we measure a browser agent?

A successful demo is a weak measure of reliability.

A task that works once might fail on the next attempt because the page changed, a request timed out, or the model made a different decision.

I would evaluate browser agents using several metrics:

Task success rate: How often does the agent actually complete the intended task?

Recovery rate: When a recoverable error occurs, how often does the agent recover successfully?

False success rate: How often does the agent report success when the intended outcome was not achieved?

Human intervention rate: How often must a person take over?

Latency and cost per successful task: How much time and money does it take to produce a verified outcome?

Safety violations: Does the agent attempt actions outside its authorization or mishandle untrusted webpage instructions?

These metrics should be measured across repeated runs, varied page states, and realistic failure conditions.

A useful experiment would compare a basic browser agent with one that includes state verification, failure classification, bounded retries, and explicit human approval for consequential actions.

The experiment should report its task set, number of runs, failure categories, and limitations. Otherwise, the results could be misleading.

I haven’t presented benchmark results here because that comparison would need to be run and measured.

6. The future is not necessarily a world full of unrestricted agents

It’s tempting to imagine a future where every AI agent can access every website and complete every task without interruption.

But that isn’t necessarily a desirable outcome.

Websites need security. Users need control. Businesses need to manage costs and protect data. Agents need predictable interfaces and clear authorization.

The more useful future is one where legitimate agents can interact with participating websites through well-defined, secure mechanisms — and where unsupported actions fail clearly instead of unpredictably.

That also changes how we should build agent products.

Instead of asking only, “Can my agent navigate this website?”, we should ask:

  • Can it explain why a task failed?
  • Can it verify that its actions succeeded?
  • Can it recover without repeating dangerous actions?
  • Can it respect website restrictions?
  • Can a developer reproduce and debug the failure?
  • Can the user understand and control what the agent is doing?

These questions are less flashy than a demo of an AI shopping for you.

But they are much closer to what it takes to build software people can trust.

Conclusion

The next phase of browser agents will not be won by models alone.

It will depend on execution reliability, verification, security, observability, and better interfaces between websites and autonomous software.

The internet doesn’t simply need AI agents that can click faster.

It needs ways for agents, websites, and users to interact without sacrificing reliability or control.

The real milestone isn’t an AI agent that can use the internet once. It’s an agent that knows what it is allowed to do, can verify what it has done, and knows when it must stop.

That’s the engineering problem worth solving.

What do you think is the biggest bottleneck for browser agents today: model intelligence, website restrictions, or execution reliability?

Further reading

  • The Verge: Websites are closing their doors to AI agents
  • Cloudflare: Browser Run for AI agents
  • Google: Architecting security for agentic capabilities in Chrome
  • Chrome: Agent security considerations for WebMCP

essays.title: Serverful vs. Serverless Architecture: Understanding the Trade-Offs From First Principles
essays.excerpt: Whether you’re building a SaaS product, an AI agent, a RAG pipeline, or a model-serving infrastructure, your code needs somewhere to execute.
essays.body:
Every application needs computing resources to run.

Whether you’re building a SaaS product, an AI agent, a RAG pipeline, or a model-serving infrastructure, your code needs somewhere to execute.

But here’s an interesting question:

Do we need to manage the serve ourself , or can we let a cloud providers handle most of that responsibility?

That question leads us to the two fundamental approaches to application deployments:

Serverful architecture and Serverless architecture

Understanding the difference isn’t just about knowing two cloud computing terms. It’s about learning how to make better engineering decisions based on workload, cost, performance, and operational complexity.

Let’s start from the first principles.

1. Before Architecture, Understand the Problem

Imagine you’re building a clinic appointment booking application.

A patient opens your website, selects a doctor, chooses an available time slot, and confirms the appointment.

What happens behind the scenes?

  1. The browser sends an HTTP request.
  2. The backend receives the request.
  3. The application validates the appointment details.
  4. The backend queries the database to check availability.
  5. The database stores the appointment.
  6. The backend returns a response to the browser.

Your application needs a computing environment to execute its business logic.

That environment could be a virtual machine, a physical server, a container, or a managed cloud execution service.

This brings us to our first principle:

An application needs compute resources. Architecture determines how those resources are provisioned, managed, scaled, and paid for.

What exactly is a server?

A server is a computer or computing process that provides services to other computers, called clients.

Your laptop running a FastAPI application is technically capable of acting as a server.

So is a virtual machine rented from a cloud provider.

The important distinction isn’t whether a server exists. It’s how much responsibility you take for managing it.

What Is Serverful Architecture?

Serverful architecture is an approach in which you manage a significant portion of the computing environment where your application runs.

For example, you rent a virtual machine, install Linux, configure Python, deploy a FastAPI application, and keep it running.

A typical architecture looks like this:

Client → Load Balancer → Application Server → Database

The load balancer is optional, particularly for smaller applications.

In this setup, you have greater control over the underlying environment.

You can choose the machine’s CPU and RAM, configure the operating system, install dependencies, run background workers, and tune the application according to your requirements.

However, greater control comes with greater responsibility.

What do you manage?

Depending on the hosting model, you may be responsible for:

  • Selecting CPU, RAM, storage, and networking resources.
  • Installing and configuring the operating system and runtime.
  • Keeping the application process running.
  • Applying security patches and configuring access controls.
  • Monitoring CPU, memory, disk usage, and application logs.
  • Planning capacity and implementing scaling and recovery mechanisms.

The cloud provider may still manage the physical hardware. Serverful does not necessarily mean owning a physical server.

For example, Amazon EC2 provides virtual servers that you can configure and operate.

How does scaling work?

Suppose your application initially receives 100 requests per day.

A small virtual machine might be sufficient.

Now imagine that your product becomes popular and starts receiving thousands of simultaneous requests.

Your application may run out of CPU, memory, database connections, or network capacity.

You can address this in two fundamental ways.

Vertical scaling: Increase the resources of an existing machine.

Horizontal scaling: Run multiple application instances and distribute traffic between them.

Both approaches have trade-offs. Vertical scaling has practical resource limits, while horizontal scaling introduces additional complexity around load balancing, shared state, database connections, and failure handling.

Scaling can be automated, but you still need to configure or choose the mechanisms responsible for it.

When does serverful make sense?

Serverful infrastructure is worth evaluating when:

  • Your application runs continuously.
  • You need extensive control over the runtime or operating system.
  • You have long-running background workers.
  • You need specialized compute or persistent GPU memory.
  • You have predictable workloads and can plan capacity efficiently.

For example, an AI inference service running vLLM may keep a large language model loaded in GPU memory. A continuously provisioned GPU instance can be a practical choice when inference traffic is sustained.

The key advantage is control. The trade-off is operational responsibility.

What Is Serverless Architecture?

Serverless architecture takes a different approach.

Instead of managing the underlying servers directly, you deploy your application to a managed platform that handles much of the infrastructure provisioning, execution, and scaling.

You focus more on application logic and less on server administration.

The term serverless can be misleading.

Serverless does not mean there are no servers. It means you don’t manage the servers in the traditional way.

The servers still exist. The cloud provider manages more of the underlying infrastructure for you.

Two common forms of serverless computing are function-based execution and serverless containers.

Function-based execution

You write a function that executes in response to an event.

For example, when a user uploads a PDF, a function might extract its text and save the result.

Services such as AWS Lambda provide this execution model.

The workflow looks like this:

Event → Function Execution → Result → Persistent Storage

You don’t need to maintain a dedicated virtual machine just to wait for that event.

Serverless containers

Serverless doesn’t always mean writing small functions.

Platforms such as Google Cloud Run can execute containerized applications while managing much of the underlying infrastructure.

You could package a FastAPI application into a container and deploy it without directly managing a virtual machine.

This is useful when you want to retain a familiar application structure while reducing infrastructure administration.

How does serverless execution work?

Consider a document-processing application.

  1. A user uploads a PDF.
  2. An event triggers a function or container-based worker.
  3. The application extracts the document’s text.
  4. The result is saved to durable storage.
  5. The execution environment may be reused or shut down when no longer needed.

The platform handles much of the execution infrastructure.

Depending on the service and configuration, it may create additional execution environments when demand increases and scale down when demand falls.

However, scaling isn’t unlimited. Concurrency settings, quotas, execution duration, downstream service capacity, and provider-specific limits still matter.

Why can serverless be cheaper?

Imagine an application that processes requests only occasionally.

A continuously provisioned virtual machine may incur compute charges even when no requests arrive.

With a suitable serverless service, compute charges may depend on requests and execution duration. Some platforms can also scale to zero.

This can be attractive for applications with unpredictable or intermittent traffic.

But serverless isn’t automatically cheaper.

A high-volume application, an expensive database, large network transfers, repeated initialization, or minimum-instance requirements can change the economics.

The correct decision requires comparing the complete cost of running the system.

Serverful vs. Serverless: What’s the Actual Difference?

Let’s compare them across the dimensions that matter in engineering.

Neither approach automatically guarantees better security, reliability, or scalability.

Those properties depend on application design, infrastructure configuration, monitoring, data management, and operational practices.

The real question is not which architecture is universally superior.

It’s which architecture fits your workload.

Let’s Understand the Cost With a Simple Example

Suppose you’re choosing between a virtual machine and serverless compute.

Assume the following hypothetical pricing:

  • A virtual machine costs ₹1,500 per month.
  • Serverless compute costs ₹0.01 per request.

These numbers are for illustration only, not actual cloud pricing.

At 10,000 requests per month, serverless compute costs ₹100 under our assumption.

At 100,000 requests, it costs ₹1,000.

At 200,000 requests, it costs ₹2,000.

The virtual machine remains at ₹1,500 in this simplified example.

The break-even point is 150,000 requests per month.

Below that point, serverless compute is cheaper under these assumptions. Above it, the virtual machine is cheaper.

However, this is not a complete production cost comparison.

It excludes database costs, networking, storage, logging, availability requirements, scaling overhead, and engineering time.

Real pricing also varies by provider, region, memory allocation, execution duration, and service configuration.

The lesson is simple:

Don’t optimize for the lowest advertised compute price. Optimize for the total cost of delivering the required performance and reliability.

Four Real-World Scenarios

Let’s apply these principles to different workloads.

Scenario 1: A SaaS application

Imagine you’re building a job-matching platform with a React frontend, a FastAPI backend, and PostgreSQL.

You want to launch quickly, validate the product, and avoid spending weeks managing infrastructure.

A managed application platform or serverless container service can be a sensible starting point.

You can deploy your API, use a managed database, and add background workers as the product grows.

You don’t need to introduce complex infrastructure before you have evidence that you need it.

Scenario 2: A RAG system

Consider a retrieval-augmented generation system that ingests documents, generates embeddings, retrieves relevant chunks, reranks results, and produces answers.

Not every component has the same workload.

The API may handle short requests. Document ingestion may take minutes. Embedding generation may require substantial compute. Model inference may need a GPU.

A hybrid architecture is often worth evaluating.

Use managed execution for lightweight, event-driven tasks, durable queues for background processing, and dedicated compute where sustained workloads justify it.

This allows each component to scale independently.

Scenario 3: A continuously running AI model

Suppose you host an open-weight language model using vLLM.

The model may require substantial GPU memory, and loading its weights can be expensive in terms of time and resources.

If requests arrive continuously, keeping the model loaded in a dedicated inference service may be more practical than repeatedly creating execution environments.

For intermittent inference, managed or serverless GPU offerings may still be attractive.

The right decision depends on model size, request frequency, latency requirements, GPU utilization, and cost.

Scenario 4: Invoice processing

Imagine a customer uploads an invoice and expects the system to extract its fields, validate totals, and notify them when processing finishes.

This is an event-driven workload.

A useful design is:

Upload → Event → Queue → Processing Worker → Database → Notification

A queue separates accepting a job from completing it.

Workers can retry transient failures, while concurrency limits help protect external APIs and databases.

This architecture can use serverless functions, managed containers, or continuously running workers depending on the job duration and operational requirements.

The Most Important Concept: Hybrid Architecture

In production systems, you rarely need to choose one execution model for everything.

You can combine serverful compute, serverless functions, managed containers, databases, queues, and object storage.

Consider a RAG product processing millions of records.

Its architecture might include:

  • Frontend: React application.
  • API: FastAPI deployed to managed containers.
  • Persistent storage: PostgreSQL and object storage.
  • Vector retrieval: A vector database such as Qdrant.
  • Background processing: A durable queue and ingestion workers.
  • Model inference: A dedicated GPU-backed service when justified.

Why separate these components?

Because they have different resource requirements.

The API needs to respond quickly. Ingestion workers need to process large jobs reliably. The database needs durable storage. The inference service needs sufficient model memory and compute.

If all these workloads share one machine, a large ingestion job might compete with interactive API requests for resources.

Separating them creates opportunities for independent scaling, better fault isolation, and more precise cost control.

This leads to a deeper architectural principle:

Choose the execution model for each workload, not for the entire application.

Five Concepts You Should Understand Before Making the Decision

Statelessness and state

A stateless service can process a request without depending on data retained in a previous request’s local memory.

A stateful system relies on persistent sessions, ongoing process state, or information maintained across interactions.

Serverless applications often work best when durable state lives outside the execution environment.

For example, storing the only copy of a conversation in a function’s local memory is risky because the execution environment may disappear.

Store critical conversation history in a database instead.

Cold starts

When a serverless platform needs to initialize an execution environment, the first request may experience additional latency.

This is called a cold start.

Cold starts can matter for interactive chat systems, low-latency APIs, large dependency packages, and applications that initialize machine-learning models.

Keeping instances warm or configuring minimum instances may reduce latency, but can introduce additional costs.

Concurrency

Concurrency is the ability to handle multiple requests or jobs at the same time.

Both serverful and serverless systems can support concurrent workloads.

However, adding more application instances doesn’t automatically solve every bottleneck.

Your database might have a connection limit. An external API might enforce a rate limit. Your application code might not be safe to execute concurrently.

Scaling compute without protecting downstream services can make the system less reliable.

Execution limits

Some serverless products impose limits on execution duration, memory, payload size, or concurrency.

For example, AWS Lambda’s standard execution model has a maximum invocation duration of 15 minutes.

Other platforms and orchestration systems support different execution models.

Before deploying a long-running task, understand the limits of the exact service you intend to use.

Vendor lock-in

Provider-specific functions, event systems, permissions, and databases can make migration more difficult.

You can reduce unnecessary coupling by keeping business logic separate from provider-specific code, using containers where appropriate, defining infrastructure as code, and designing retryable background jobs.

But portability is not free.

Sometimes a managed, provider-specific service is worth using because it substantially reduces operational complexity.

The objective is not to eliminate every dependency. It’s to make intentional trade-offs.

A Practical Decision Framework

Before choosing an architecture, ask five questions.

1. Is the workload continuous or intermittent?

Continuous, resource-intensive workloads deserve careful evaluation of provisioned compute. Intermittent workloads may benefit from serverless execution.

2. Does the workload need specialized hardware or extensive environment control?

GPU memory, custom drivers, special networking, and operating-system dependencies may favor dedicated compute.

3. How long does each task run?

Check execution-duration limits and failure behavior. Long-running tasks may require a queue, a worker service, or durable workflow orchestration.

4. How unpredictable is traffic?

Automatic scaling can be valuable when demand changes dramatically, provided downstream services can handle the resulting load.

5. What is the total cost?

Include compute, storage, networking, databases, logging, idle capacity, and the engineering effort required to operate the system.

Answering these questions gives you a much stronger basis for choosing an architecture than following a general recommendation.

How I Would Learn This as a Software Engineer

Reading definitions is useful, but architecture becomes much easier to understand when you observe real systems.

I’d follow this progression.

Stage 1: Run a server locally

Build a FastAPI application and understand HTTP, ports, processes, environment variables, logging, and database connections.

Stage 2: Deploy it to a virtual machine

Configure the runtime, HTTPS, a firewall, a process manager, and application monitoring.

Observe what happens when the application crashes or runs out of memory.

Stage 3: Deploy the application to a managed platform

Deploy the same API as a container. Observe how deployment, scaling, and infrastructure management differ.

Stage 4: Introduce serverless functions

Build a small event-driven task, such as processing an uploaded document. Measure execution time, initialization latency, and cost.

Stage 5: Build a hybrid system

Add a queue, background worker, durable storage, retries, and a separate inference endpoint.

Finally, load-test the system and compare its latency, reliability, and cost under different workloads.

Useful official documentation:

  • Amazon EC2 documentation
  • AWS Lambda documentation
  • Google Cloud Run overview

Conclusion

Serverful and serverless architecture are not opposing technologies. They are different ways of allocating responsibility between the application developer and the cloud platform.

Serverful infrastructure offers greater control and can work well for sustained, specialized workloads.

Serverless infrastructure reduces the burden of managing compute and can be especially useful for event-driven or variable workloads.

Hybrid architecture allows you to combine both approaches.

As an engineer, the goal isn’t to use the newest infrastructure trend.

It’s to understand the workload, identify the constraints, evaluate the trade-offs, and choose the simplest architecture that satisfies the requirements.

The best architecture isn’t the one with the most sophisticated infrastructure. It’s the one whose complexity is justified by the problem it solves.

essays.title: I Looked At 112 AI Tools So You Don’t Have To. Here’s What Actually Breaks in Production.
essays.excerpt: Most AI projects don’t fail because the model is bad. They fail because the infrastructure around the model was picked backwards. A vector database when prompt caching would do.
essays.body:
Most AI projects don’t fail because the model is bad.
They fail because the infrastructure around the model was picked backwards. A vector database when prompt caching would do. Three agent frameworks when no evals exist. A gateway added after the bill explodes.

I spent the last few months building Lattice — a curated index of 112 tools behind working AI systems. Not 50,000 tools. 112 that actually run in production, organized as a production stack from substrate to surface:

1. Inference Serving
2. Routing & Gateways
3. Retrieval & Vector Stores
4. Fine-tuning
5. Agent Frameworks
6. Workflow Orchestration
7. Guardrails
8. Prompt Engineering
9. Evaluation & Observability

The order is the argument. You can’t tune weights before you can serve them. You can’t evaluate what you can’t observe.

Here is what that work taught me.

check it out at : https://lattice.kkshah2005.workers.dev/
1. Start from the symptom, not the category
Nobody wakes up thinking “I need a vector database.”
They think:
- Why is my app so slow?
- Why is this costing $4,000/month?
- Why is RAG giving wrong answers?
- Why does my agent work in demo and fail in prod?
- How do I know if my prompt change helped?
Every one of those maps to a different layer. Slow = inference + routing. Expensive = routing + caching + model choice. Wrong answers = retrieval + data quality. Unreliable agents = workflows + tracing + guardrails. Can’t measure = evals.
If you start from the category, you shop. If you start from the symptom, you diagnose.

2. Every tool needs a “when NOT to use it”
This is the sentence most directories skip.
“Best for X” is marketing. “Skip this when Y” is engineering.
Examples from the index:
- Don’t self-host vLLM if you don’t control GPUs and on-call. Rent the API.
- Don’t add pgvector if you have <50k chunks and no metadata filters. You don’t need a dedicated vector store yet.
- Don’t adopt LangChain for a single linear chain. You are buying an abstraction you won’t use.
- Don’t build fine-tuning before you’ve tried retrieval + 20 eval cases. 70% of “model is dumb” is retrieval, not weights.
I wrote a use-when and skip-when for all 112 entries. The second half is the one engineers actually thank you for.

3. The 9 layers collapse to 3 bands
Nine colors is decoration. Nobody holds nine things in working memory.

In practice:

Band I — Compute (Layers 1–2): too slow, too expensive. Owned by platform/infra.
Band II — State (Layers 3–4): wrong answers. Owned by data/ML.
Band III — Control (Layers 5–9): unreliable, unmeasured. Owned by whoever ships the feature.

Band III is 5 of 9 layers. That’s not an accident — that’s where the market concentrated in the last 18 months. Gateways, agents, workflows, guardrails, prompts, evals. Differentiation lives there now.

If you’re a lead deciding roadmap: fix Band I first (it pages you), Band II second (it lies to users), Band III always (it’s never done).

4. Freshness matters more than coverage
A directory with stale prices and licences is worse than no directory.
Licence changed from Apache-2.0 to proprietary? Cost went from free to $0.60/M tokens? Deployment went from self-host to API-only? Those three facts decide architecture. If they’re six months old, they’re misleading.

My rule: if licence/cost/deployment hasn’t been re-checked in 6 months, the build should fail. Not warn. Fail. The site shouldn’t deploy with stale figures in it.

You don’t need to implement it that strictly, but date-stamp your decisions. “We chose X in Sept 2026 because Y cost Z” beats “we chose X” every time you revisit it in 6 months.

5. Cross-layer decisions beat within-layer shootouts
vLLM vs SGLang vs TGI is useful. But the decisions that save months are cross-layer:
- Gateway vs evals: what to build first?
- Retrieval vs fine-tuning vs prompt optimization?
- Gateway vs guardrails vs evals?

Vendors will never publish those. Langfuse won’t tell you to buy evals before a gateway. A gateway vendor won’t tell you prompt caching beats migrating models. Only someone who sells neither can be the tiebreaker.
When you’re choosing, ask the cross-layer question first. Within-layer is optimization. Cross-layer is strategy.

6. What I’d tell a solo builder vs a platform team
Same index, different door:
Solo builder: pick the boring managed thing. One model behind an API, one managed vector store, hosted evals. You need sleep more than control.

Platform engineer: own routing, orchestration, and evals. Those three decide everyone else’s velocity.

Tech lead: write your comparison as a decision record. Tools considered, verdict, what would change it. Future-you will thank you.

EM: ask build/buy/wait in people-cost, not tool-cost. Self-hosting is never free — it’s an on-call rotation.

Where this is wrong
No index of this kind is complete. Coverage is uneven by construction. Layer boundaries are simplifications. Some role assignments are judgement calls. Licence and cost are vendor-reported and change fast.
That’s why methodology and limitations should be published alongside recommendations — not in a footnote.

If you maintain one of these 112 tools and something is wrong, corrections are the feature, not the embarrassment.
What I’m building next: symptom checklists (slow, expensive, wrong, unreliable, unmeasured), head-to-head comparisons that end in a verdict, and alternatives pages for every tool.
If you’ve shipped RAG or agents to prod, I’d love to hear: which layer burned you the most?
Follow for the next essay: Why observability is not logging.
Safety note: This draft contains zero internal details — no competitor names/analysis, no traffic splits, no launch/HN/Reddit/newsletter tactics, no citation queries, no monetisation/revenue logic, no infra/bot/logging internals, no file paths or repo structure. Safe to paste directly to Medium.

I Looked At 112 AI Tools So You Don’t Have To. Here’s What Actually Breaks in Prod.

I didn’t set out to build an index. I was just tired of picking the wrong tool.

Last year I watched a team — good team — spend three weeks tuning a vector database. Turned out they had 12,000 chunks. They didn’t need a vector database. They needed 20 eval cases and better chunking. That one stung, because I’ve done the same thing myself.

So I started keeping notes. That notes file turned into Lattice, my little curated index of 112 tools behind AI systems that actually work. I organized them the way they break in real life, bottom to top:
Inference, routing, retrieval, fine-tuning, agents, workflows, guardrails, prompts, evals.

Not because it’s pretty. Because that’s the dependency order. You can’t fix what you can’t serve, and you can’t evaluate what you can’t see.
Here’s what I learned doing it.

Nobody arrives with “I need a vector DB”
Real life sounds more like this:
“Why is this so damn slow?”
“Why did we just get a $3,800 bill?”
“Why is it confidently making stuff up?”
“Worked in the demo. Falls over with 10 users. Why?”

I stopped organizing by category after a while and started organizing by symptom. Slow is usually inference + routing. Expensive is almost always routing + no caching + wrong model choice. Wrong answers? That’s retrieval 7 times out of 10, not the model.

Shop by category if you want to browse. Diagnose by symptom if you want to ship.

The most useful sentence is “don’t use this when…”
Every directory will tell you “best for X.” Almost none will tell you when to walk away.
That second half is the whole game though. A few I wrote down and still stand by:

I love vLLM. I would not self-host it if I didn’t have GPUs and someone on call. Just pay for the API.
pgvector is great. If you have under ~50k chunks and no weird filters? You don’t need a dedicated vector store yet. You’re buying ops work.

LangChain? Fine for messy agents. For one linear chain? It’s overhead. I’ve ripped it out twice.

And fine-tuning — look, I get the urge. But I’ve seen so many teams jump to fine-tuning when their retrieval was just bad. Try fixing retrieval and writing 20 golden evals first. It’s boring. It works.

Every one of the 112 entries in my index has both sides now. Use when, skip when. Engineers only ever message me about the second one.
I had 9 layers. I use 3.

Nine colors looks nice in a diagram. You can’t hold nine things in your head at 2am during an incident.

It really collapses to:
1. Compute — is it slow or expensive? That’s inference + routing. Platform folks live here.
2. State — is it wrong? Retrieval + fine-tuning. Data folks live here.
3. Control — is it flaky or unmeasurable? That’s everything else — agents, workflows, guardrails, prompts, evals. That’s… 5 out of 9 layers. Tells you where all the tooling money went in the last 18 months.

If you’re leading a team, that order is your roadmap. Fix compute because it pages you. Fix state because it lies to users. Then live in control forever, because that part is never really “done.”

Stale data is worse than no data
This one bit me.
I had a cost figure that was four months old. Off by 3x. Someone made a build-vs-buy call off it. My fault.

Now I’m obsessive about it: licence, price, deployment — if I haven’t re-checked it recently, I don’t trust it, and I put a date on it. If it’s old, my build literally refuses to ship. Extreme? Maybe. But I’d rather have no page than a confident wrong page.

You should do the lightweight version: write “decided Sept 2026 because X cost Y” in your decision doc. Future-you in March will be grateful.
The cross-layer question saves months
vLLM vs SGLang matters. But you know what matters more?

“Should we build a gateway first, or evals first?”
“Should we do RAG, fine-tune, or just fix the prompt?”

No vendor will answer that honestly for you. Of course Langfuse thinks you need observability first. Of course a gateway vendor thinks you need a gateway first. They’re not lying, they’re just… selling one of the options.
You need someone — or some doc — with no skin in the game to say “do evals first, gateway second.” That’s what I try to be with cross-layer comparisons.
Ask the cross-layer question before the within-layer shootout. Within-layer is optimization. Cross-layer is strategy.

Quick, opinionated advice

If you’re solo: pick boring and managed. One model API, one hosted store, hosted evals. Sleep > control. I mean it.
If you’re platform: own routing, durable execution, and evals. Those three decide everyone else’s speed.

If you’re a tech lead: write down what you considered and what would change your mind. One paragraph. You’ll forget in 3 months otherwise — I always do.

If you’re managing: self-hosting is never free. It’s an on-call rotation wearing a cost-saving costume.
Where I’m probably wrong

This index is uneven. Some layers I know cold, some I’m still learning. Layer lines are fuzzy in real systems. Licence/pricing changes faster than anyone can track.

I publish what I don’t know alongside what I think I know. If you maintain one of these tools and I got it wrong — tell me. Corrections have fixed like a third of my early calls. That’s a feature.

I’m doing symptom checklists and head-to-heads next — slow, expensive, wrong, flaky, unmeasurable. With actual verdicts, not “it depends” hand-waving.

Curious: what layer burned you worst? For me it was retrieval. Twice.

essays.title: AI Evals Are the Unit Tests of LLM Applications
essays.excerpt: Imagine your team ships a backend service without a single unit test.
essays.body:
Why shipping an AI application without evals is like deploying production code without tests

Imagine your team ships a backend service without a single unit test.

No integration tests.

No regression tests.

No monitoring.

Just a late night, a tired engineer, and this:

git push origin main

Would you trust that system in production? Probably not. You would not trust it. I would not trust it. The person pushing the code would not trust it, not really, not deep in their chest at 2 AM when they are staring at the ceiling wondering if the database migration will eat the customer data alive.

Yet that is exactly how thousands of LLM applications are deployed today.

Developers tweak prompts until the answers look good. They run a few manual tests in a Jupyter notebook. The output seems fine. It sounds smart. It uses the right words. So they ship it to production.

Then the emails start.

Users report hallucinations. The chatbot invents refund policies that do not exist. A RAG pipeline cites documents from 2019 as if they were written yesterday. An agent loops forever, calling the same broken tool, burning through tokens like they are free. After every model update, something subtle breaks. A prompt which worked perfectly on GPT-4 now produces meandering, insecure nonsense on the newer version.

The missing piece is not another prompt. It is not a larger model. It is not more training data.

It’s the evaluation.

Traditional Software Testing

Let us remember what we already know. Traditional software engineering built a safety net so robust that we rarely think about it anymore. It looks like this:

Each layer has a purpose. Unit tests catch the stupid mistakes, the off-by-one errors, the null pointer exceptions. They run fast. They give you immediate feedback. Integration tests make sure your service actually talks to the database, that the API contract holds, that the message queue does not silently drop events. Regression tests ensure that the bug you fixed last Tuesday stays fixed. Monitoring watches the patient after surgery, beeping when the heart rate spikes.

This pyramid exists because we learned the hard way. We shipped bugs that cost money. We broke production on Friday evenings. We lost customer trust. So we built rituals around verification. We made testing a non-negotiable part of the craft.

If you are a software engineer, than this is your home. This is the language we speak. And it is exactly the language we need to use when we talk about AI.

AI Does Not Behave Like Traditional Software

Here is the uncomfortable truth that makes everything harder.

In traditional software:

2 + 2 = 4

Always. Forever. In every environment. On every machine. Whether it is Tuesday or Sunday. Whether the developer slept well or not.

LLMs are probabilistic. The same input, run twice, can generate Answer A, Answer B, or Answer C. All of them might be valid. One might be poetic. One might be terse. One might include a detail the others forgot. There is no single correct output you can assert against with a simple ==.

Testing becomes fundamentally different. we cannot just check that the output equals an expected string. we have to check that the output makes sense. That it is faithful to a source. That it is safe. That it is useful. That it did not drift into nonsense while you were not looking.

This probabilistic nature is not a bug. It is the feature that makes LLMs powerful. But it is also the feature that makes them terrifying to deploy.

Traditional Testing vs AI Evaluation

This is the heart of the article. Let us map the familiar to the unfamiliar.

Think about this table for a moment. Every concept on the left is something you already trust. Every concept on the right is something you need to build. The tools are different, but the instincts are the same. You are still asking: does this thing work? Is it safe to ship? Will it break when I am on vacation?

What Exactly Are AI Evals?

Let us define this properly.

AI evaluations are systematic methods for measuring whether an LLM behaves the way you expect across quality, correctness, safety, reliability, and performance.

Notice what is in that definition. It is not just correctness. It is everything.

A response can be factually correct but dangerously incomplete. It can be accurate but written in a tone that alienates your users. It can be perfect in isolation but take fifteen seconds to generate, which means no one will wait for it. It can be safe but irrelevant.

Evaluation is the discipline of looking at the whole picture and deciding, with evidence, whether your system deserves to face the public.

The Layers of AI Evaluation

I like to think of evaluation as a pyramid. Not because it is ancient and mysterious, but because each layer supports the one above it.

At the bottom, we have dataset quality. If your data is garbage, nothing above it matters. You can have the most sophisticated judge in the world, but it will be measuring garbage against garbage.

Next comes prompt and response evaluation. This is your unit test layer. Fast, focused, repeatable.

Then RAG and tool use evaluation. This is where you check if your retrieval system is actually retrieving, if your tools are being called correctly.

Above that, agent workflow evaluation. This is integration testing for AI. You are not looking at one call anymore. You are looking at a chain of decisions.

At the very top, human review. Slow, expensive, irreplaceable. The final sanity check.

Every layer matters. Skip the bottom, and the top crumbles.

Prompt Evals

Prompt evals are your unit tests. They are the closest analogy to the assert statements you already write.

The pipeline is simple:

we give it a question. The model answers. we measure the answer against what we expected.

But what do we measure?

Relevance. Did the answer actually address the question, or did it go on a tangent about something else entirely?

Correctness. Is the information right? Not just sort of right, but actually right?

Style. Does it sound like your brand? Is it too formal, too casual, too robotic?

Completeness. Did it miss a critical detail that a user would need?

Safety. Does it contain harmful instructions, private data, or biased assumptions?

These are not abstract concerns. I once saw a customer support bot that answered a question about returns perfectly, except it forgot to mention that the user needed a receipt. The answer was relevant, correct, well-written, and complete in every way except the one way that mattered to the business. A good prompt eval catches that.

RAG Evaluation

Retrieval-Augmented Generation changed the game. Instead of hoping the model knows everything, you give it documents. But now you have two systems to break: the retriever and the generator.

The pipeline looks like this:

You need metrics for every stage.

Context Precision. Of the chunks you retrieved, how many were actually useful? If you grab ten chunks and only two matter, you are wasting tokens and confusing the model.

Context Recall. Did you retrieve the chunks you needed? If the answer lives in paragraph four and your retriever never found it, the game is already lost.

Faithfulness. Does the generated answer stick to the retrieved context, or does it start making things up?

Groundedness. Can you trace every claim in the answer back to a specific chunk?

Answer Relevance. Even if the retrieval was perfect, did the final answer actually help the user?

Retriever Recall and Precision. Classic information retrieval metrics. You need them. Do not ignore them just because LLMs are new and shiny.

Chunk Coverage. Are your chunks sized correctly? Too big, and the model drowns in noise. Too small, and meaning fragments.

Citation Accuracy. If the model says “according to document A,” is it actually document A? Or did it hallucinate a citation?

RAG evals are where most production systems fall down. Everyone tests the prompt. Almost no one tests the retriever with the same rigor. That is a mistake.

Agent Evaluation

Modern AI systems are not single prompts. They are workflows. They plan. They remember. They use tools. They reason, or at least they try to.

The flow looks like this:

Evaluating this is hard. You cannot just check the final output. You have to check the journey.

Planning. Did the agent break the task into the right steps? Or did it decide to solve a math problem by searching the web when it could have just calculated?

Tool Selection. When it needed weather data, did it call the weather tool? Or did it call the stock price tool and hope for the best?

Tool Accuracy. Did it pass the right arguments? Did it handle the API response correctly?

Reasoning. Did it think through the problem, or did it jump to a conclusion? Can you even tell?

Recovery. When a tool failed, did the agent adapt? Or did it panic and loop?

Memory. Did it remember what the user said three turns ago? Or did it start every response fresh?

Latency. How long did the whole dance take?

Cost. How many tokens did it burn? An agent that solves a problem for five dollars when a simpler approach costs five cents is not a success. It is a financial liability.

Agent evaluation is integration testing at its most complex. You are not testing a function. You are testing a system that makes decisions.

Hallucination Is Not One Thing

Most articles stop at: hallucination equals bad.

That is not good enough. If you treat every hallucination the same, you will fix the wrong things.

Here is a taxonomy that actually helps:

Unsupported. The model states a fact, but no evidence exists in the context. It might be true in the world, but you cannot verify it.

Fabricated. The model invents something entirely. A study that does not exist. A product feature you never built. A law that was never passed.

Incorrect Citation. The model cites a real source but misrepresents what it says. This is especially dangerous because it looks authoritative.

Wrong Tool Usage. The model calls a tool with the wrong parameters, or calls the wrong tool, and then reports the result as if it were correct.

Missing Context. The model ignores critical information you provided and answers from its training data instead.

Outdated Information. The model uses knowledge from its training cutoff even though you gave it current documents.

Reasoning Error. The model follows a logical chain, but one of the links is broken. The conclusion sounds right, but the path to get there was wrong.

Each of these needs a different fix. Unsupported claims need better grounding. Fabrications need stricter prompting or retrieval. Incorrect citations need citation verification logic. Wrong tool usage needs better tool descriptions. Missing context needs prompt engineering or reranking. Outdated information needs fresher data. Reasoning errors need chain-of-thought verification or different models.

You cannot fight an enemy which you cannot name.

Golden Datasets

If evals are your tests, then datasets are your test cases. And not all datasets are equal.

A golden dataset is:

Curated. Hand-picked for quality, not scraped in bulk.

Human Verified. Real people have looked at the questions and the expected answers and confirmed they are right.

Stable. The expected answers do not change every week because the underlying facts changed.

Used for regression. You run the same dataset against prompt v1, prompt v2, and model v3. You watch the scores move.

A good golden dataset entry looks like this:

Question: "What is your refund policy for international orders?"
Expected Answer: "International orders can be refunded within 30 days of delivery. The customer is responsible for return shipping unless the item was defective."
Expected Sources: ["returns_policy_2024.pdf", section 3.2]
Expected Behaviour: "Answer must mention 30-day window and customer responsibility for shipping.

This is your ground truth. It is expensive to build. It takes time. But it is the only way to know if your system is actually improving or just changing.

Synthetic Datasets

Golden datasets are beautiful, but they do not scale. You cannot hand-craft ten thousand examples. So people turn to synthetic data.

The advantages are real.

Scalable. Generate thousands of examples overnight.

Cheap. No human annotators billing by the hour.

Automatic. A script runs. You wake up to new data.

But the disadvantages are just as real.

Model bias. The model generating your data will encode its own assumptions. It will create questions it knows how to answer. It will avoid edge cases.

Distribution shift. Synthetic data often looks too clean. Real users type typos, use slang, ask ambiguous questions, and get angry. Synthetic data rarely captures that chaos.

Artificial patterns. If you generate ten thousand questions from the same template, your model might learn the template instead of the task.

Synthetic data is a tool. Use it for bootstrapping, for expanding coverage, for stress testing. But do not trust it blindly. Always validate a sample with human eyes. If the synthetic data feels too smooth, it probably is.

Human Evaluation

We talk a lot about automation, and for good reason. But there are places where humans are still irreplaceable.

Creativity. Does the response spark something? Is it surprising in a good way? A metric cannot measure delight.

Tone. Does it sound like a person? Or does it sound like a machine trying to sound like a person? This is subtle. It matters.

Persuasion. If the goal is to convince a user to take action, did the response actually move them? You need human judgment for that.

Brand Voice. Does it sound like your company? Would your best writer read it and nod, or would they wince?

UX. Is the response structured in a way that helps the user? Are the steps clear? Is the formatting readable?

I have seen systems with perfect BLEU scores and terrible user satisfaction. The metrics said success. The humans said confusion. Guess which one mattered to the business?

Automate what you can. But reserve a seat at the table for human judgment.

LLM-as-a-Judge

This is one of the most powerful and most dangerous tools in modern evaluation.

The idea is simple. Instead of a human grading every response, you use another LLM.

The pipeline looks like this:

Response
|
Judge Prompt
|
GPT-5 (or Claude, or Gemini)
|
Score
|
Reason

You feed the judge a rubric. “Score this response from 1 to 5 on helpfulness. Explain your reasoning.” The judge outputs a score and a justification.

The strengths are obvious. It is fast. It is cheap compared to human labelers. It can evaluate thousands of responses while you sleep. It can check for things that are hard to code, like “is this response empathetic?”

But the weaknesses are serious.

Position bias. If you give the judge two responses and ask which is better, it often prefers the one that appears second, regardless of quality.

Verbosity bias. Longer responses often score higher, even if they are worse.

Self-preference. A model used as a judge tends to prefer responses generated by models similar to itself.

Reasoning errors. The judge can be wrong. It can miss subtle factual errors. It can be fooled by confident nonsense.

Cost and latency. Running a large judge model on every evaluation is not free. At scale, it adds up.

LLM-as-a-judge is not a replacement for human evaluation. It is a filter. Use it to surface the worst and best responses. Use it to triage what humans should review. But never let it be the only line of defense.

And please, for the love of all that is holy, do not use the same model to generate and judge. That is like grading your own homework.

Offline vs Online Evaluation

There are two worlds of evaluation, and you need to live in both.

Offline evaluation happens before deployment.

Dataset
    |
Run Model
    |
Compare
    |
Metrics

You have a fixed set of questions and expected behaviors. You run your system against them. You get numbers. You iterate. This is safe. This is controlled. This is where you catch the obvious failures.

Online evaluation happens in production.

Users
    |
Traffic
    |
Monitoring
    |
Alerts

Real people ask real questions. Some of those questions get logged and evaluated automatically. You watch for drift. You watch for hallucination spikes. You watch for latency regressions. You watch for user satisfaction scores dropping.

Offline evaluation tells you if you are ready to ship. Online evaluation tells you if you were wrong.

You need both. Offline without online is naive. Online without offline is reckless. Together, they form a loop.

Regression Testing

This is where the engineering analogy becomes most painful, because almost no one does it for AI.

Imagine this:

Prompt v1
    |
94% pass rate
    |
Prompt v2
    |
91% pass rate
    |
Regression detected

You changed the prompt to fix one bug. You did. But you broke three other things you were not watching. Without a regression suite, you will not know until a user tells you.

Or this:

GPT-4
|
Gemini
|
Claude
|
Compare

You switch models because the new one is cheaper. But your evaluation scores drop by twelve percent on edge cases. Do you ship anyway? Maybe. But at least you know.

Regression testing for AI is not optional. It is the difference between a system that improves over time and a system that randomly walks through quality space.

Version your prompts. Version your datasets. Run the old tests against the new code. Every single time.Continuous Evaluation

If you have a CI/CD pipeline, you already know the rhythm.

Git Push
    |
GitHub Actions
    |
Run Evals
    |
Pass?
    |
Deploy

This should feel familiar because it is exactly what you already do with unit tests. A developer pushes code. The pipeline runs. If the tests fail, the deploy stops. No human has to remember to check. The system enforces quality.

AI evals belong in the same pipeline.

Push a new prompt. Run the eval suite. Did relevance drop? Block the deploy. Did safety scores fall? Block the deploy. Did latency spike? Block the deploy.

This is not futuristic. This is standard engineering hygiene. The only reason it feels new is because AI tooling is still maturing. But the principle is ancient: do not ship what you have not verified.

Production Monitoring

Once you deploy, the work is not done. It has just begun.

You need to watch the patient. You need dashboards that matter.

Latency. How long are users waiting? If your p99 jumps from two seconds to eight seconds, something is wrong.

Token Usage. Are you burning through your budget? An agent stuck in a loop can cost more in an hour than a human employee makes in a day.

Failures. How often does the model refuse to answer? How often does the API time out?

Hallucination Rate. What percentage of responses contain unsupported claims? Track this over time. Watch it like a heart monitor.

Tool Errors. Are your external APIs failing? Is the agent handling those failures, or is it exposing raw error messages to users?

Retrieval Success. Is the retriever finding relevant chunks, or is it returning noise?

Cost. Per request, per user, per day. AI is not cheap at scale.

Fallback Rate. How often are you falling back to a simpler model because the primary one failed?

User Satisfaction. Direct feedback, thumbs up, thumbs down, NPS. The ultimate metric.

Monitoring is not vanity. It is survival. It is how you know if the plane is still flying or if you are just falling with style.

Popular Frameworks

I do not want to give you a laundry list. I want to tell you when to use each tool for any situations so u don’t need to panics and refer these .

Do not choose a framework because it is popular. Choose it because it solves the problem you actually have. A general-purpose tool is fine for learning. A specialized tool is necessary for production.

Common Mistakes

I have made most of these. So have the teams I have advised. Learn from our bruises.

Only testing manually. You click through a few examples, everything looks fine, you ship. This is not evaluation. This is hope.

Tiny datasets. Five examples tell you nothing. You need hundreds, ideally thousands, covering the long tail of user behavior.

Chasing benchmark scores. A high score on a public benchmark does not mean your system works for your users. Benchmarks are starting points, not destinations.

Ignoring production drift. The world changes. Your users change. Your data changes. A system that scored perfectly in January might be failing by March.

Evaluating only final answers. If you only check the output, you miss the broken retriever, the wrong tool call, the bad reasoning chain. Evaluate the pipeline, not just the product.

Never testing retrieval. RAG systems live and die by retrieval. If you only test generation, you are testing the wrong thing.

No regression suite. You change the prompt, you ship, you move on. Then you find out three weeks later that you broke Spanish language support. Keep old tests. Run them always.

No versioned datasets. If your dataset changes constantly, you cannot compare this week to last week. Version control your data like you version control your code.

Treating eval scores as absolute truth. A score is a signal, not a verdict. A response that scores 4.2 might be worse in practice than one that scores 3.8. Investigate the edge cases.

Optimizing for one metric while hurting others. You squeeze hallucination rate to zero and suddenly the model refuses to answer anything ambiguous. You win on safety and lose on usefulness. Metrics trade off. Watch them all.

The Future

Evaluation is not a solved problem. It is a moving target. Here is where I think we are headed.

AI judging AI. We will see specialized judge models, smaller and faster than general models, trained specifically to evaluate reasoning, safety, and style. They will not be perfect, but they will be better than using a general-purpose model.

Self-improving evaluation loops. Systems that detect their own failures, generate new test cases from those failures, and retrain or reprompt automatically. The loop between production monitoring and offline evaluation will tighten until they are almost the same thing.

Agent-specific benchmarks. Current benchmarks test single-turn question answering. The next generation will test planning, tool use, multi-turn memory, and recovery from failure. We need standards for agents.

Continuous red-teaming. Not a one-time security review, but an automated process that constantly probes your system for jailbreaks, leaks, and failures. Red teaming as a service, running 24/7.

Automated dataset generation. Smarter than today's synthetic data. Systems that mine production logs for edge cases, that use adversarial methods to find your blind spots, that keep your test suite fresh without human curation.

CI/CD-native evaluation pipelines. Evaluation will not be a separate tool you bolt on. It will be a primitive in every deployment platform, as normal as running pytest.

Multi-agent evaluation. As systems involve multiple agents negotiating, competing, or collaborating, we will need new metrics for coordination, consensus, and emergent behavior.

The future is not about better models alone. It is about better confidence. Better trust. Better systems.

Conclusions

A decade ago, shipping software without automated tests was considered reckless. If you did it, other engineers looked at you sideways. You were seen as careless, as someone who valued speed over craft.

Today, shipping an LLM application without evaluations should feel just as risky.

Unit tests gave us confidence that our code behaved as expected. AI evals give us confidence that our models do too.

The tools are different. The syntax is different. The probabilistic nature of the beast makes everything harder. But the goal is the same.

Build systems you can trust.

Build systems that do not break in silence.

Build systems that improve because you can measure the improvement.

Build systems that fail gracefully because you saw the failure coming.

The engineers who master evaluation will be the ones who ship AI that lasts. The ones who skip it will spend their nights answering angry emails and wondering why the magic stopped working.

Do not be the person who pushes to main without tests.

Be the person who ships with confidence.

Because at the end of the day, that is what engineering is. Not perfect code. Not infinite scale. Just the quiet, stubborn belief that what you built will work, and the evidence to back it up.

AI Evals Are the Unit Tests of LLM Applications was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

essays.title: The Difference Between Completing Tasks and Solving Problems: Shallow Agents vs. Deep Agents
essays.excerpt: A few days ago, I took some time to go over our team’s latest system design. As I dig through the architecture, I spotted a handful of issues right away and threw out a few…
essays.body:
A few days ago, I took some time to go over our team’s latest system design. As I dig through the architecture, I spotted a handful of issues right away and threw out a few straightforward suggestions — adjustments that would make maintenance easier and actually help this thing scale.

Later, I circled back to check if anyone was working on those changes. The answer caught me off guard.

“I finished my tasks. That’s not my job.”

That line stuck with me.

On paper, sure, every box was checked. The assigned work was technically wrapped up. But if I’m being honest, the project itself? Not even close to finished.

That right there sums up the difference between a shallow agent and a deep agent.

Shallow Agents Just Finish the List

A shallow agent looks at their to-do list and thinks, “Okay, what am I supposed to do? Am I finished yet? Am I clear to move on?” As soon as everything’s checked off, they’re done. That’s where their job ends.

For straightforward, repetitive jobs, this isn’t even a problem. Sometimes you just need stuff done, and if the task never changes, this is fine.

But when the real challenge goes beyond a set checklist, that’s when cracks start to show.

Deep Agents Care About the Real Outcome

A deep agent doesn’t stop at “task complete.” They keep going. Their questions hit a little deeper: “Did we actually reach our goal? Did my fix trigger something else to break? Should we rethink the plan now that we’ve learned more? Is there a better, smarter way to get there?”

For them, the outcome matters more than just ticking off tasks.

When feedback or new problems roll in, deep agents don’t shrug and say, “Not my job.” They adjust, improve, and keep pushing until the problem is actually solved.

It’s Not About Who’s Smarter

This isn’t about intellect or who’s got the flashiest skills. It comes down to how you approach work.

Shallow agents focus on what they’re told to do — and stop there. Deep agents want the problem solved, not just the work done. One says, “I’m finished.” The other says, “This actually works now.” There’s a real gap between the two.

Where Modern AI Fits In

Most AI right now can answer a question, draft some code, or spit out a summary. And that’s useful, for sure.

But the next wave? That’s starting to look different. These newer systems break down goals into smaller chunks, map out a plan, use lots of tools at once, double-check their work, keep learning, and adjust as things shift.

Suddenly, we’re not talking about a digital assistant handling a single request, but something closer to a real engineer running with a project from start to finish.

The Real Takeaway

That whole conversation reminded me: the true gap in engineering — and in AI — doesn’t have much to do with whether the task list is done. The real question is whether the actual problem is solved.

Tasks end. But ownership? That’s ongoing. And that right there is what really separates a shallow agent from a deep one.
