essays.title: How Memory Works in Python: The Complete Guide (From Variables to Garbage Collection)
essays.excerpt: Ever wonder what really happens when you type x = 10 in Python? Where does that value actually live? Does Python make a copy, or just point to it?
essays.body:
Ever wonder what really happens when you type x = 10 in Python? Where does that value actually live? Does Python make a copy, or just point to it? And how does Python know when it’s time to free up memory? Let’s walk through the whole life cycle of a Python object — from the moment you create it to the moment it disappears. We’ll keep it visual, practical, and friendly for beginners, but we’ll also peek behind the scenes at how CPython does its magic.

Python’s famous for its simple syntax, but there’s a complex memory system working behind the curtain. Every time you create a variable, call a function, add something to a list, or delete an object, Python’s handling a whole bunch of low-level operations: grabbing memory, managing references, tuning performance, and cleaning up after itself.

Understanding how Python handles memory pays off in a bunch of ways:
– You write faster, more memory-efficient code.
– Bugs caused by mutable objects? Easier to avoid.
– You get the difference between shallow copies and deep copies.
– Reference mysteries? Easier to debug.
– You’re better prepped for Python interviews.
– And you’ll actually start to appreciate how CPython is put together.

In this article, we’ll trace a Python object’s journey — from the moment you bring it into existence, right up to the point Python clears it away.

What Happens When Python Starts?
When we start a Python program, the interpreter sets up a whole environment:
– Built-in objects
– A global namespace
– The memory allocator (PyMalloc)
– The garbage collector
– The module loader
– The execution stack

Everything we create lives inside this environment.

Everything’s an Object
Seriously — almost everything in Python is an object:
– Integers
– Strings
– Lists
– Dictionaries
– Functions
– Classes
– Modules
All of them.

Every object has three core traits:
– Identity — its memory address (check with id())
– Type — what kind of object it is (type())
– Value — the actual content inside

Try this:
x = 42
print(id(x))
print(type(x))
print(x)

That’ll show us the unique identity, the type, and the value of x.

Variables Are References, Not Boxes
Here’s a key idea: Python variables don’t actually contain values. They just point to objects.

x = 10
y = x

Now both x and y point to the same object in memory. That’s why assigning a list to another variable doesn’t make a copy — you’re just making another reference. On the other hand, if you reassign an immutable object (like a number or a string), you create a new object instead.

Stack vs Heap Memory
Python splits up where it stores stuff:
– The stack holds function calls, local references, and execution frames.
– The heap holds actual objects — lists, strings, dictionaries, class instances.

So whenever you create a new object, it lands on the heap. The variable that points to it, though, lives in a stack frame or namespace.

Object Creation and Memory Allocation
Look at this:

numbers = [1, 2, 3]

Here’s what Python does:
1. Allocates heap memory.
2. Builds a list object.
3. Puts the list’s elements in memory.
4. Establishes a reference called numbers.
5. Links that reference to the new list.

That’s why if you tweak a mutable object, every variable that points to it sees the change.

Mutable vs Immutable Objects

Immutable: int, float, bool, tuple, str.
Change one, you actually get a new object.

x = 5
x = 8

Here, x stops pointing to 5 and moves on to 8 — the original 5 object isn’t touched.

Mutable: list, dict, set, custom classes.
You can add, change, or remove stuff inside them, and all references see the effect.

a = [1, 2]
b = a
a.append(3)

Both a and b now point to the same, updated list: [1, 2, 3].

Object Identity, Type, and Value

You can always check:
x = “Python”
print(id(x))
print(type(x))

When we compare objects:
== checks if the values are equal.
is checks if they’re literally the same object in memory.

Reference Counting

CPython (the default Python) watches how many references exist to every object. Every time you make a new reference (assign a variable, pass to a function, store in another object), the count goes up. Remove a reference, the count drops. When there are zero references left, Python instantly frees that memory.

Garbage Collection

Now, reference counting works, but it can’t solve everything. If two objects reference each other (a cycle), but nothing else points to them, they won’t get cleaned up automatically.

Example:

class Node:
pass
a = Node()
b = Node()
a.next = b
b.next = a

Delete both a and b, and they still point to each other. To fix this, CPython uses a cyclic garbage collector — it roots around periodically for these “unreachable” cycles and reclaims their memory. It groups objects by “generation,” checking newer ones more often (since older objects probably aren’t stuck).

PyMalloc: The Memory Allocator

CPython doesn’t ask the operating system for memory every time it creates an object. Instead, it uses PyMalloc — a sort of memory manager with arenas, pools, and blocks. Small objects come from these blocks, which makes creation really fast and avoids memory clutter.

Object Interning and Caching

Python tries to save memory by reusing common immutable objects — small integers, popular strings, interned identifiers. For example:

a = 10
b = 10
print(a is b)

This usually prints True, because both variables point to the same little integer cached by Python.

Function Calls and Stack Frames

Each time you call a function, Python makes a new stack frame. Local variables, arguments, the return address, and the current execution state all live inside that frame. When the function finishes, the frame disappears. If nothing else is pointing to the local objects, Python frees their memory soon after.

Shallow vs Deep Copy

Python gives you two ways to copy objects:

Shallow copy: copy.copy(obj) — makes a new container, but nested objects are still shared.
Deep copy: copy.deepcopy(obj) — remakes everything, including all nested objects, so you get a fully independent structure.

Getting this wrong is what causes sneaky bugs with lists of lists or dictionaries inside dictionaries.

Memory Optimization Tips

If you want your programs to use less memory and go faster:
– Use tuples instead of lists for data you won’t change.
– Pick generators for big data sets.
– Delete unnecessary references when you’re done.
– Reuse objects where you can.
– For classes with tons of instances, try using __slots__.
– Profile memory with tracemalloc.
– Don’t copy objects needlessly.
– Pick the right data structure for the job.

Common Python Memory Myths

Myth: Variables store values.
Truth: Variables store references to objects.

Myth: del always frees memory.
Truth: Memory is only reclaimed when the last reference is gone.

Myth: Python doesn’t have garbage collection.
Truth: CPython uses both reference counting and cyclic garbage collection.

Myth: is and == are the same.
Truth: == checks for equal values, while is checks for object identity.

Bringing It All Together

When you write:

numbers = [1, 2, 3]

Python:
– Grabs memory with PyMalloc,
– Creates the list object on the heap,
– Fills in the list elements,
– Sets up your variable reference,
– Tracks reference counts,
– Manages execution via stack frames,
– Releases references when you’re done,
– Frees memory through reference counting or the garbage collector.

You don’t see any of this happening, but every Python app — big or small — relies on it.

Conclusion

Python’s memory management is a balancing act: simple to use, but sophisticated underneath. Once you understand objects, references, stack frames, the heap, mutability, reference counting, garbage collection, and PyMalloc, you’ll start to see how Python really runs your code.

This insight helps you write cleaner, faster code, makes bugs easier to fix, and even gets you comfortable with more advanced stuff like CPython internals and optimization. Next time you jot down x = 10, just remember — Python’s memory system is quietly making sure that one line is efficient, safe, and completely effortless for you.

essays.title: The Boy Who Built Machines While Looking for a Place to Belong
essays.excerpt: If you walked into a classroom and looked around, you probably wouldn’t notice him. He’s not the loudest one. He’s not the one surrounded by friends.
essays.body:
If you walked into a classroom and looked around, you probably wouldn’t notice him.
He’s not the loudest one.
He’s not the one surrounded by friends.
He’s not the one constantly taking selfies or planning weekend trips.
He sits quietly, listens more than he speaks, and when the lecture ends, he picks up his bag and leaves.
To most people, he’s just another engineering student.
But inside his head, entire worlds are being built.

At twenty-two years old, in the final year of engineering, he spends his nights building AI agents, architecting memory systems, experimenting with vector databases, contributing to open source, planning research papers, and imagining products that don’t exist yet.
While many are busy chasing grades, he dreams about creating things that outlive him.
He isn’t interested in just getting a job.
He wants to build.
He wants to create.
He wants to leave behind something that whispers,
“Someone was here, and they changed the world a little.”

His GitHub profile isn’t just a collection of repositories.
It’s a diary.
Every commit represents another evening spent alone with a laptop while the rest of the world seemed to move together.
Projects like AgentForge, SENTINEL-CLI, Aegis, his own vector database — these aren’t just software.
They’re conversations.
Because sometimes, code is easier to understand than people.
Machines don’t ghost you.
Algorithms don’t judge you.
A compiler tells you exactly what’s wrong.
Humans rarely do.

He often wonders why friendship seems so effortless for everyone else.
Groups form naturally around him.
People laugh together.
They make plans.
They share stories.
And somehow, he always feels like the extra person.
Not disliked.
Not hated.
Just… optional.
The kind of friend people greet with a smile but forget to call.
The one who initiates every conversation.
The one who notices that if he stopped sending messages, silence would answer back.
Over time, that silence starts speaking.
It tells him stories.
It says,
“Maybe they don’t really need you.”
“Maybe their lives would be exactly the same without you.”
“Maybe you’re just passing through everyone else’s story.”

Then there is another silence.
The one that comes from never really having someone who chooses you.
At twenty-two, he has never had a girlfriend.
He has watched classmates fall in love, break up, laugh together, and create memories while he remained an observer.
He tried talking.
Sometimes people replied.
Sometimes they disappeared.
Sometimes they blocked him.
After enough unanswered messages, a person doesn’t simply stop texting.
They begin to question whether they deserve a reply at all.
Eventually, he stopped trying.
Not because he stopped caring.
Because rejection becomes exhausting.

The strange thing is that people would probably describe him as ambitious.
They would see the GitHub activity.
The LinkedIn posts.
The research ideas.
The AI projects.
The late-night coding sessions.
They would think,
“This guy has everything figured out.”
But they wouldn’t see the nights when the laptop closes.
When the room becomes quiet.
When the screen goes dark.
And he wonders why building intelligent machines feels easier than building one genuine human connection.

But there is one person who breaks through all of it.
He’s known him since school. Childhood. Back when life was simple and they were just two kids growing up in the same classrooms, the same stupid phases, the same everything. Somewhere along the way, he became the only person he doesn’t have to translate himself for.
He’s in MBBS now. Different city. Different world. Buried in anatomy and pharmacology while he sits here building AI agents at 2 AM like some kind of mad scientist.

They don’t talk every day anymore. Sometimes weeks go by. Distance changes things — not because anyone stops caring, but because life grabs you by the collar and doesn’t let go.
But when he sends him something — a random thought at midnight, a screenshot of broken code, a question he’s too embarrassed to ask anyone else — he answers. Not always immediately. But he answers. And somehow that’s enough.
Last week he was stuck. Not on code. Just stuck. The kind of stuck where you’re lying in bed at 3 AM and your brain is running in circles and you can’t find the off switch. He texted him. Three words. “You awake?”
He called ten minutes later.
It was past midnight in his city too. He had an exam in six hours. He called anyway.

They talked for maybe twenty minutes. Nothing big. Just him making fun of him for overthinking. Him making fun of him for memorizing a thousand bones. But after they hung up, he could sleep. That’s what he does for him. He doesn’t fix anything. He just makes the noise stop.
He is the one friend who texts first.
He is proof that he exists in someone else’s world.
He is the reason that silence doesn’t always win.

Yet despite everything, he keeps building.
He learns about decision trees and entropy.
He studies machine learning.
He plans research papers in AI for the railway sector.
He dreams of open-source communities.
He imagines strangers across the world contributing to ideas that began in his small room.
Perhaps he doesn’t realize it yet, but that’s hope.
People who have truly given up don’t plan futures.
They don’t build.
They don’t create.
They don’t imagine.
He does all three.
Every single day.

Maybe the greatest misunderstanding of his life is that he thinks he is looking for a girlfriend.
He isn’t.
Not really.
What he is looking for is belonging.
Someone who says,
“Sit here.”
Someone who messages first.
Someone who asks,
“How’s your project going?”

Someone who chooses him without needing a reason.
The absence of that kind of connection hurts more than the absence of romance ever could.
But here’s what he doesn’t fully see yet:
He already has that.

In one person. In a childhood friend who chose him before either of them understood what choosing meant. In an MBBS student in another city who still picks up the phone at midnight. In the only person who makes him feel like he’s not passing through everyone’s life like a ghost.
Maybe that’s not the same as what everyone else has. Maybe it’s not a group chat that buzzes all day or a relationship that everyone posts about. But it’s real. And it’s his.

There is a quote often attributed to programmers:

“Every programmer has two lives: the one they live and the one they build.”
For him, those two lives have become deeply intertwined.
He builds systems with memory because he fears being forgotten.
He builds intelligent agents because he longs for conversations that understand him.

He contributes to open source because somewhere inside, he hopes to find people building toward the same future.
But somewhere in another city, his best friend is studying to save lives. And some nights, that’s enough. Knowing that out there, someone is doing something hard too. Someone gets it. Someone would notice if he disappeared.

One day, this chapter will end.

College corridors will disappear.
The friend groups that seem permanent today will scatter across cities and countries.
The people who never texted first will fade into old contact lists.
And perhaps one evening, while working late with a small team of builders somewhere, someone will casually ask,

“Hey Kunj, we’re grabbing dinner after this. You coming?”
It will seem like an ordinary question.
But for the boy who spent years believing he was the extra person, it will quietly heal a part of him that nobody ever knew was broken.
And somewhere, his MBBS friend will be doing the same thing — saving a life or laughing with his own people — and neither of them will know that on the same night, they’re both still holding each other up from a distance.

Until then, he keeps building.
One commit.
One idea.
One late-night conversation with his own thoughts at a time.

Because beneath the loneliness, beneath the silence, beneath the feeling of being unseen, there is still a dreamer who believes that somewhere in this enormous world, there are people who will understand him.
And maybe the story of his life isn’t about the friends he doesn’t have.

Maybe it’s about the thousands of lives he will touch through the things he creates.

Maybe the quiet boy in the last bench isn’t a side character after all.

Maybe he’s simply at the beginning of his own story.

And maybe — just maybe — he already has the one person who proves he’s real.

essays.title: A Comprehensive Guide to Key Topics in Statistics-Part 1
essays.excerpt: Welcome to our journey into the world of statistics! Picture a dense forest, each tree a piece of data. Without a guide, it’s overwhelming.
essays.body:
Welcome to our journey into the world of statistics! Picture a dense forest, each tree a piece of data. Without a guide, it’s overwhelming. Statistics is that guide, turning chaos into clarity. Whether you’re a data scientist or a curious beginner, join us as we explore the fascinating landscape of statistics. Let’s dive in!

Introduction

Statistics is a crucial field of study that involves collecting, analyzing, interpreting, presenting, and organizing data. It plays a vital role in various domains such as science, business, social sciences, and more. By understanding statistical concepts, one can make informed decisions, predict future trends, and gain insights into complex problems. This guide aims to cover the essential topics in statistics that are fundamental for anyone looking to delve into this fascinating field.

Descriptive Statistics

Descriptive statistics are used to summarize and describe the main features of a dataset. They provide simple summaries about the sample and the measures, which are essential for understanding the data at hand.

Definition and Importance

Descriptive statistics help us make sense of large volumes of data by reducing lots of data into a simpler summary. This summarization is crucial for communicating large amounts of data efficiently and effectively.

Measures of Central Tendency

Measures of central tendency provide a single value that attempts to describe a set of data by identifying the central position within that set.

  • Mean: The mean, or average, is calculated by summing all the values in a dataset and then dividing by the number of values.​​
  • Median: The median is the middle value in a dataset when the values are arranged in ascending order. If the dataset has an even number of observations, the median is the average of the two middle numbers.
  • Mode: The mode is the value that appears most frequently in a dataset. A dataset may have no mode, one mode, or multiple modes.

Measures of Dispersion

Measures of dispersion describe how similar or varied the set of observed values are for a particular variable.

  • Range: The range is the difference between the highest and lowest values in a dataset.
  • Variance: Variance measures how far each number in the set is from the mean and thus from every other number in the set.

Standard Deviation: The standard deviation is the square root of the variance and provides a measure of the average distance between the values of the data in the set and the mean.

Data Visualization

Data visualization is the graphical representation of information and data. By using visual elements like charts, graphs, and maps, data visualization tools provide an accessible way to see and understand trends, outliers, and patterns in data.

  • Histograms: Used to represent the distribution of numerical data.
  • Box Plots: Provide a five-number summary of the data: minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile, and maximum.
  • Scatter Plots: Useful for showing the relationship between two variables.

For those eager to learn more, here are some references to get you started:

  • Khan Academy: Statistics and Probability
  • Coursera: Statistics with Python Specialization
  • Stat Trek: Teach Yourself Statistics
  • Krish Naik’s YouTube Channel: Statistics and Machine Learning Tutorials

RL-A2A Enhanced is an open-source project that solves all these challenges — combining secure, real-time agent-to-agent (A2A) communication with multi-AI integration (OpenAI, Claude, Gemini), advanced visualization, and production-ready deployment. 🎉 Conclusion

RL-A2A Enhanced isn’t just another AI project — it’s a leap forward for secure, intelligent, and collaborative agent systems. If you want to build the future of AI, start here.

essays.body:
Agentic AI: Future Directions — Opportunities and Cybersecurity Applications

Artificial Intelligence had grown from being just a buzzword into being part and parcel of our lives. From voice assistants, recommendation algorithms to bots seamlessly intertwined with modern technology, this leaves the place to the next addition in the grand play- — Agentic AI.

In contrast, the system, while it achieves relative high-grade autonomy, must not be confused with agentic AI because agentic AI, being contrasted to classical AI, doesn’t need the system to process tasks under some predefined rules or supervised learning. Apart from its decision-making capability, it possesses adaptiveness to act upon the observed scenario for its goals instead of only analyzing and understanding it. Just imagine any AI system that can determine a goal, learn dynamically without being plugged, and support coordination in teamwork with humans without any flaws. That is what is ambitiously promised by Agentic AI.

Let’s dive deeper into the future of Agentic AI, its potential uses across various industries, and most importantly, its game-changing applications in cybersecurity.

What is Agentic AI, Exactly?
The line of artificial intelligence has evolved further into agentic AI. It is phenomenal when it comes to handling specific tasks, such as image recognition, natural language processing, or data analysis. But Agentic AI goes beyond all that. It emulates human agents in the capacity to perceive contexts, make decisions, and act without constant human intervention.

While a regular AI chatbot would respond to frequent queries coming from customers based on some preloaded scripts, its counterpart agentic AI chatbot could monitor customer sentiment in real time, decide on the best action — like offering a discount or escalating a complaint — and change its behavior to achieve better outcomes over time. This self-directed nature just opens the roof to a realm of applications everywhere, from hospitals to financial circles.

Future Examples of Agentic AI
The roles of Agentic AI are of such magnitude-so far, in fact, from what we come across. And now, let’s cover some futuristic utilizations:

1. Onboard Learning
Imagine studying where teachers, being custom AI tutors, literally learn and, therefore, adapt to the different pace at which each student learns and his other characteristics. Agentic AI might be that personal mentor who, in knowing one struggles at times, hones in on key points, even suggesting when breaks are required. It’s not just completing problems in the worksheet for the sake of filling up the pages; that’s understanding and teaching to love.

2. Health Transforming
Agentic AI could be extremely transformative in terms of healthcare change for the diagnosis and overall patient care. Now, let’s come to the realm of cybersecurity, where Agentic AI could have the most critical effect. In a world that is getting increasingly digital, cyber threats get increasingly sophisticated. Agentic AI will be able to work alone as an autonomous threat hunter, constantly monitoring the networks for open vulnerabilities and suspicious activities. Among the greatest threats in cybersecurity lies the fact that cyber attackers are adapting their methods rapidly. The Ethical Balancing Act
As with any powerful technology, Agentic AI has its share of ethical considerations. With such a system that acts autonomously, it raises questions of accountability and control. For example, who is accountable if an AI system makes a decision that leads to unintended consequences? How do we ensure its actions actually conform to human values and ethical standards?

These are concerns that particularly arise in cybersecurity. For example, how do we prevent Agentic AI from accidentally locking users out of systems or taking overtly sensitive actions to the point where operations could be severely disrupted? Ensuring Agentic AI remains a force for good is going to take a great deal of transparency, robust testing, and setting clear boundaries.
